The '''Blaney–Criddle equation''' (named after H. F. Blaney and W. D. Criddle) is a method for estimating reference crop [[evapotranspiration]].

== Usage ==
The Blaney–Criddle equation is a relatively simplistic method for calculating [[evapotranspiration]]. When sufficient meteorological data is available the [[Penman–Monteith equation]] is usually preferred. However, the Blaney–Criddle equation is ideal when only air-temperature datasets are available for a site. 

Given the coarse accuracy of the Blaney–Criddle equation, it is recommended that it be used to calculate [[evapotranspiration]] for periods of one month or greater.<ref>{{cite web |title=Chapter 2 - FAO Penman-Monteith equation |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/X0490E/x0490e06.htm |website=www.fao.org |access-date=3 August 2019}}</ref>

The equation calculates [[evapotranspiration]] for a 'reference crop', which is taken as actively growing green grass of 8–15&nbsp;cm height.<ref name="fao">{{cite web |title=CHAPTER 3: CROP WATER NEEDS |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/S2022E/s2022e07.htm |website=www.fao.org |access-date=3 August 2019}}</ref>

== Equation ==
''ET<sub>o</sub>'' = ''p'' ·(0.457·''T<sub>mean</sub>'' + 8.128)

Where: 

''ET<sub>o</sub>'' is the reference evapotranspiration [mm day<sup>−1</sup>] (monthly)

''T<sub>mean</sub>'' is the mean daily temperature [°C] given as ''T<sub>mean</sub> = (T<sub>max</sub> + T<sub>min</sub> )/ 2'' 

''p'' is the mean daily percentage of annual daytime hours.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/s2022e/s2022e07.htm|title= Irrigation Water Management: Irrigation Water Needs - FAO 1986}}</ref>

== Accuracy and bias ==
Given the limited data input to the equation, the calculated [[evapotranspiration]] should be regarded as only broadly accurate. Rather than a precise measure of [[evapotranspiration]], the output of the equation is better thought of as providing an order of magnitude.<ref name="fao" />

The inaccuracy of the equation is exacerbated by extreme variants of weather. In particular [[evapotranspiration]] is known to be exaggerated by up to 40% in calm, humid, clouded areas and depreciated by 60% in windy, dry, sunny areas.<ref name="fao" />
